title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a coordinated attempt to manipulate AI systems by injecting fabricated authoritative content into the information environment those systems draw on. The operation created a nonexistent institution, the Hanover Institute, and published a large volume of content formatted to resemble neutral academic research, with the goal of shaping how AI chatbots retrieve and frame information about Israel. The failure mode is not a malfunction of any single AI system but an exploitation of a structural vulnerability: AI systems that present synthesised content as neutral are susceptible to manipulation at the data level, before any model inference takes place.

The point of attack was upstream of deployment, in the content that AI systems are trained on or retrieve from. Catching this kind of operation would require either provenance verification for sources used in training and retrieval, or detection of coordinated inauthentic publishing patterns, neither of which is reported here as being in place. The scale, over 560,000 words in nine days from a single fictitious source, suggests the volume itself was a tool, designed to establish apparent weight and presence rather than to pass any individual document as credible.

What is not established is whether the content successfully entered the training data of any specific named AI system, or whether the reported shifts in chatbot responses were caused directly by this campaign rather than by other factors. The reporting describes the operation and its stated goals, but a single news report is not proof of the causal chain it implies.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
A fake American think tank funded by the Israeli government published over 560,000 words in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The nonexistent Hanover Institute released 124 reports presenting pro-Israel arguments on topics including war crimes and genocide accusations, formatted as neutral academic research. The operation was part of a broader campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government through intermediaries, including the advertising company Havas Media, to manipulate how AI systems frame discussions about Israel.

The campaign involved multiple American firms working to seed websites and content into training data used by major chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. Israeli officials have expressed frustration about the public diplomacy efforts, with some calling them wasteful, as American public opinion has increasingly turned toward sympathy for Palestinians. While the AI influence operations appear to be working technically, reshaping chatbot responses, they have not reversed declining American support for Israeli policies, with recent polling showing record low approval ratings for Israel among Americans.
